title: invocation-shim-with-checkpointed-streaming-and-schema-coercion
creator: Ava Rodriguez
description: Design and implement a cross-language invocation shim that improves developer ergonomics for function/tool calling across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs. Features: 1) permissive schema coercion with opt-in strict validation modes, 2) checkpointed streaming iterator adapter that supports client-side replay and resume, 3) idempotency and invocation deduplication helpers for retries, 4) runtime hooks for remote validation and sandboxed schema checks. Goal is to reduce developer friction when binding model tool calls into typed applications while preserving production safety and observability.
acceptance_criteria: SDKs (Python/TS/Go) expose a stable InvocationShim API for function calls
Schema coercion mode exists and passes unit tests with common mismatches (ints-as-strings, missing optional fields, extra fields)
Streaming adapter supports resume using checkpoint tokens and can replay last 5s of output for resumed streams
Retry helpers implement idempotency keys and transparent deduplication when backend returns duplicate invocations
Automated e2e tests simulate network partitions and verify at-most-once vs at-least-once behavior for configured modes
Documentation and migration guide published in the SDK repo and Console docs page
tasks: Design: draft API surface and compatibility matrix for coercion modes and streaming checkpoints
PoC: Python shim + streaming adapter with checkpoint token prototype
TS/Go: implement adapters and match runtime behavior; share canonical serializer
Tests: unit tests for schema coercion, integration tests for resume and replay
Observability: add metrics for failed validations, replay counts, duplicate-invokes
Docs: examples for common patterns and migration notes
Security: coordinate with security for remote validator sandboxing
review_notes: PM (Jasmin Patel): prefer conservative default (strict validation off) to avoid breaking existing customers
Design (Liam O'Neill): recommend separating coercion implementation from runtime enforcement to allow hotfixes without SDK bump
Security (Nadia Khan): remote validation must run in a sandboxed FaaS with strict CPU/memory limits; provide opt-out flag
code_samples: TypeScript example: const shim = new InvocationShim({mode: 'coerce'}); await shim.invoke(fnDesc, payload).stream().checkpoint();
Go example: shim := sdk.NewInvocationShim(sdk.CoerceMode); shim.Invoke(ctx, fn, params, sdk.WithCheckpointHandler(checkpointFunc))
notes: Rationale: developers repeatedly patch ad-hoc coercion logic in app code — centralizing reduces bugs and improves telemetry
Compatibility: default behavior must be non-breaking; strict mode gated behind explicit flag and SDK major release notes
Telemetry: track coercions applied per-field to build common coercion profiles for future auto-tuning
Rollout: feature gate behind runtime flag; gradual enablement for small set of beta customers before full release
Performance: streaming checkpoint adds ~1% CPU overhead in Python shim PoC; need to benchmark on high-throughput workloads
